video_title: How to Survive Being a Mall Santa
text: It's Christmas time, and you're enjoying some exciting things. The season is changing, you're decorating a tree, and eggs are being nogged. And a very special man is coming to malls and shopping centers around the world. Santa Claus. You might see the rotund, happy man, sitting there talking to kids and posing for photos, and think that his job is simple. But it takes a lot of work and preparation to be a mall Santa. The chances are that Santa's a graduate of Santa University, a four-day course in Arvada, Colorado. To attend, potential Santas must pass background and security checks. They go through interviews, where they're asked about their experiences with children, fondest memory of playing Santa, and most importantly, what Christmas means to them. If they're successful, the Santa students will learn the ethics of playing Santa, how to stay in character, some inside tips on playing the big man, and how to handle tough questions and situations. video_title: How to Survive Being a Mall Santa
text: It's your first gig as the jolly man in red. How are you going to survive this for six weeks? The most important part of playing Santa is that you must stay in character at all times. This includes outside of Santa season too. Talking to Santa can be incredibly important to a young child, so giving them the best experience possible is your top priority. Most Santas say they do it for the smiles and joy it brings to the kids, not for the paycheck. You'll need to be an expert on Santa. Be sure to know things like Mrs. Claus' name, the reindeers' names, and how to deliver presents to houses without chimneys. And stay up-to-date on Santa movies. Children might ask you why you did certain things in a movie, so you'll need to know what they're asking about. Browse a toy catalog too, so you know what a child might ask for, and talk with them about that toy. Remember, you make all of them in your workshop, so you need to know your products. Children don't always speak English, and some children can't speak at all. It helps if you speak more than one language. Students of Santa University learn the essentials of sign language as part of their training. And you'll be encouraged to learn key phrases in Spanish, or other common languages used near your shopping center gig. Communicating to a child in their native tongue can make a huge difference to them. You need to look the part. While a child might not notice that you're wearing a cheap, felt Santa suit, parents will. The best Santas invest in a hand-sewn Santa suit with white fur trim. Your clients will range from babies to children. And there may be some unforeseen accidents, such as vomiting or a surprise bathroom visit on your lap. So bring several red suits with you. A small amount of red makeup on your cheeks and nose can also help give you that jolly disposition. Santas are encouraged to have their beards professionally bleached to the Kris Kringle white. If it isn't done right, a beard can turn out yellow.

video_title: How to Survive Being a Mall Santa
text: Who wants to be mobbed at the urinal? Peeing privately also helps maintain the illusion of being Santa. Some malls have a private dressing room and bathroom for Santa. But if you don't have this luxury, find the most out-of-the-way bathroom there is. Or, ask nearby stores if they'll let you use their staff restrooms. Who's going to say no to Santa? Mall Santas have the capacity to talk to over 50,000 children in the six week period they work. That is a lot of heavy lifting, a lot of weight focused on your lap and the capacity for an large amount of germs to be around you. At the end of your shift, make sure you go home and get plenty of rest and recovery. Have heat packs to warm and relax your back and arms from lifting a child while in a sitting position. Have ice packs on hand for the bruising that can occur on your legs from the children sitting there all day. There will also be plenty of germs in your beard if the kids stoke it play with it, cough, or sneeze near it. So plan for a daily washing and styling session. Be sure to carry with you plenty of hand sanitizer. Germs can easily spread when in contact with so many children so do your best to protect both yourself and any other child from these germs. Playing Santa can be an intimidating job, but the joy it brings to thousands of children keeps the Santas coming back. Remember the Christmas spirit, and the joy you're bringing to the kids, and you can survive being a mall Santa. What if you took it one step further, and went to the North Pole? Even with your red suit on, you might not be prepared for such extreme cold. But if Santa can do it, you can do it. Just watch How to Survive Being Frozen, here on How to Survive.
